paragraphs: Chapter 6 Results Chapter abstract. This chapter reports the measured wave, the calibrated in-silico experiment, and the balanced evidence synthesis. It covers descriptives, reliability, CFA, hypothesis results, the G0/G1 contrast, calibration, the Bayesian check, joint sensitivity, topology and persona checks, component ablations, source ablation, anchor bootstrap, held-out prediction, a Gemini persona-agent pilot, and a human-gold validation of machine qualitative coding. It distinguishes measured, model-based, and legacy stress-test ndings and reports frequentist and Bayesian summaries side by side. This chapter preserves reported questionnaire results, historical respondentlevel sensitivity, qualitative themes, and a joint display, separated from the historical calibrated simulation. The interpretation of Student Rating is separated from episode evaluation and from the extended study design. Field tables and gures reproduce the measured-wave exports included in the reproducibility archive; the nal calibrated pipeline is reported separately in Section 6.12. The historical two-arm simulation and its Bayesian summary retain the original study's model summaries; their provenance is distinguished in Appendix L. A model contrast is not an observed eld intervention eect. 162

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 163 In plain terms. Read the results with three scales in mind. The evaluative Student Rating is a 17 score built from credibility and perceived-benet items. The competence-format rating is a 0100 synthetic NMLS display. Engagement is a 01 composite of raw interaction. The measured PB and star ratings are the human anchor; all other contrasts are model-based implications, not grades or human learning gains. 6.1 The Measured Wave 6.1.1 Sample Description The analytic sample comprised 52 university students, 30 male and 22 female, following eight historical exclusions from 60 collected questionnaires. The retained-ID list reproduces the sample; the precise duplicate key is examined in Section 6.4. The setting was social media radio listening associated with Uber journeys in the 6th of October City area, Giza. The export lists six institutional categories, with counts of 12, 5, 13, 3, 13, and 6. These are sample categories, not estimates of institutional populations. Reported ride duration ranged from 5 to 15 minutes. Interaction was self-reported as minimal, low, moderate, or high. 6.1.2 Descriptive Results The post-broadcast composite had a mean of 5.119 (SD = 0.867) on the sevenpoint scale. The overall star-rating mean was 3.94 on the ve-point scale. Most respondents selected four stars (40 of 52); the remaining counts were one two-star,

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 165 6.1.3 Associations Among Audience Evaluations PB was positively associated with the star rating (ρ = .671), reported interaction (ρ = .601), and ride duration (ρ = .616). The broadcaster-rating subscales were also positively associated with PB: BR, .809; SV, .952; and IQ, .946. Durationstar correlation was .309. All coecients are Spearman correlations from the supplied association export; they are not standardised regression coecients or causal eects. The very high SVPB and IQPB associations raise an interpretive question. They may reect shared audience evaluation, but they may also reect substantive overlap and common response processes. A separate star-rating block provides convergent self-report evidence, not an independent criterion of information accuracy or a demonstrated learning gain. The export stores the starPB probability as zero at its output precision; an exact zero probability is not reported here, and no unreported condence intervals are constructed from the summary alone. 6.2 Psychometric Calibration 6.2.1 Internal Consistency The broadcaster-rating battery had α = .957 overall. CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 170 6.4 Respondent-Level Recheck and Exclusion Sensitivity The inherited audit describes a respondent-level reanalysis in addition to cross-le summary checks. The les are absent from the present archive; the following is a historical account, not a fresh rerun. The 52 retained identiers reproduce the reported PB mean and SD, star mean, alpha coecients, PB item means and SDs, and six principal Spearman associations to the displayed precision. BR4 is reversed as 4 −BR4 before forming the four-item BR score. There are no missing item responses in the supplied 60-record questionnaire le. The raw le contains 16 scale items and one star rating, not 21 scale items. Removing exact duplicates on these 17 responses alone would exclude 34 records; using all non-identier questionnaire elds would exclude four. Neither rule reconstructs the historical eight exclusions. The newly supplied processing specication identies a 21-eld key: the 16 scale responses, star rating, age, ride duration, trafc category, and interaction category. Applying exact equality on those elds to the 60-record merged matrix and retaining the rst record reproduces exactly the eight exclusions and the retained 52 cases. The retained item and context values also agree with the earlier analysis matrix. Thus the earlier account species an operational lter for future reproduction; its description must not call all 21 elds scale items. This agreement does not establish when the rule was chosen, or that matching responses necessarily identify the same person. The main analysis retains the historical subset, reports all-60 sensitivity, and does not classify the excluded participants as fraudulent.

The corpus contains 60 records; 52 are linked to the retained questionnaire sample. Table 6.6 reports coding coverage, not population prevalence. Every record has at least

Theme denitions appear in Table 6.6; the chart reports coding coverage only. 6.5.1 T1: Accountable Practice and Social Endorsement The accounts oer two dierent grounds for credibility. One concerns how claims are handled: SR002 values transparent correction, SR009 values primary sources, SR0017 values neutral moderation, and SR0033 values source acknowledgment. The

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 173 recorded remark for SR002 states: Transparency in admitting mistakes builds far more credibility than pretending to be an infallible expert. These cases position credibility as something a broadcaster demonstrates in communication, rather than merely possesses as a reputation score. Other cases locate trust in peer feedback and visible community ratings (SR0012, SR0016, SR0025, SR0060). SR0012's recorded remark says, Peer reviews make it easier to trust new broadcast hoststhis is how radio should build credibility in the digital age. This is a dierent mechanism: social endorsement can guide judgment without establishing factual accuracy. T1 therefore complicates, rather than validates, a single BRS construct. Neither the account claiming that diverse viewpoints prevent polarisation (SR0042) nor the account praising trac-note accuracy (SR0056, T5) is a measurement of those claimed eects. 6.5.2 T2: Peer Voices and Socially Local Radio Student voices are described as familiar, spontaneous, and socially proximate. SR001 contrasts unedited student speech with conventional morning shows; SR0026 and SR0040 contrast conversational delivery with rehearsed radio. SR0011 connects familiar banter with feeling less isolated, while SR0036 connects peer audio notes with solidarity during nals. These meanings suggest that voice and social identication are part of evaluation, not incidental features of content delivery. The interpretation remains situated. The archive does not establish sustained changes in loneliness, campus belonging, or mental health. Nor does familiarity make a source accurate. For EST, this theme identies a plausible audience-level pathway that should not be absorbed into architecture alone: a student's prior connection to

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 174 the voices may shape the judgment of the same interface. 6.5.3 T3: A Worthwhile Ride Need Not Be an Interactive Ride The most widely coded theme concerns the t between audio and the immediate journey. Calm matters in accounts of fatigue and stress; brevity and clear structure matter when listening time is limited. SR003's recorded remark states, Audio platforms should feel like a cozy lounge rather than an aggressive ad strip. SR0014 values short segments, and SR0031, SR0041, SR0046, SR0049, and SR0054 value concise or clearly structured delivery. These are accounts of situated usefulness, not measurements of learning gain. The paired cases show why activity is an incomplete measure of value. SR003 has low recorded interaction but PB of 5.6; SR0011 also has low interaction with PB of 5.0. Conversely, SR0018 appreciates the low-key tone while giving PB of 3.0 and two stars. A favourable comment about one feature can coexist with an unfavourable overall evaluation. This does not negate the positive pooled interactionPB association; it prevents reading that association as a universal equation between visible action and worthwhile listening. 6.5.4 T4: Agency, Contribution, and Protected Access SR004's topic vote and SR0019's visible poll response are recorded instances of inuencing the communication process. Creator-oriented accounts are more tentative: SR0013, SR0024, and SR0051 ask how to contribute or express an intention to do so. Their enthusiasm is not evidence that a broadcast was subsequently produced, independently veried, or used for learning.

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 175 Participation is also conditional on access and control. SR0034 values an anonymous participation option, and SR0030 requests custom topic lters. The latter is a constructive criticism, not an observation that the feature already worked. SR0059 oers technical feedback. Together these accounts position participation as an opportunity to shape the platform, not simply a high interaction count. They inform EST-P4's proposed aordances without establishing a causal benet of those aordances. 6.5.5 T5: Relevance Grounded in Student-Lived Needs Practical topics recur: student trade (SR001), side-hustle issues (SR005), remote work (SR0038), graduate interviews (SR0044), trac (SR0056), and startup funding (SR0057). Campus updates and environmental participation appear in SR008 and SR0029. The recorded remark for SR0038 identies part-time remote work opportunities as the kind of practical content students need. Interest in a technology discussion (SR0039) and an AI-ethics debate (SR0022) indicates that relevance is not conned to immediate utility. These cases supply a reason to build and compare topic repertoires. They do not show that all members of a faculty share the same preferences. The supplied proles repeatedly connect discipline to interests; using those connections as deterministic agent rules would reproduce the archive's framing rather than test it. Topic preference should be individually grounded and capable of changing with context.

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 176 6.5.6 T6: Delivery and Interface Quality as Enabling Conditions Several accounts praise clarity, continuity, latency, or interface design. SR006, SR0021, SR0047, SR0050, and SR0058 describe audio delivery; SR0027 values visual simplicity, and SR0052 values one-tap controls. SR0037 states a conditional preference: As long as the audio doesn't cut out and the content isn't annoying, I prefer social radio over static FM noise. This is a threshold of acceptability rather than evidence that more interaction or more technical sophistication is always better. Engineering-sounding remarks remain experiential reports. No buer trace, latency benchmark, security audit, or packet-loss test follows merely from a rider describing a stream as robust. Equally, a transcript-only LLM cannot reproduce an audio-quality judgment simply by being told that the stream is excellent. Technical telemetry and listening modality must be separated in the planned agent extension. 6.5.7 Tensions, Additional Cases, and Evidential Limits The eight records outside the historical quantitative subset add two T3, two T4, three T5, and one T6 memberships. They do not introduce a seventh theme under this codebook, but that observation is not a saturation claim. Their continued inclusion prevents a numeric ltering decision from silently removing distinct qualitative accounts. The corpus is overwhelmingly favourable. Its main qualifying cases concern quiet appreciation, conditional preference, and suggested improvements rather than sustained rejection. This imbalance may reect selection, the recording process, or the social circumstances of the encounter; the present archive cannot separate

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 177 these explanations. The analysis preserves that limitation instead of construing the absence of extensive criticism as unanimous support. 6.6 Integration of Quantitative and Qualitative Findings Table 6.7 integrates evidence at the case and construct levels. It supports the interpretation that audience evaluation combines content, social cues, reception conditions, and interface experience. It does not transform a cross-sectional association into an architectural eect. CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 178 6.7 Focus-Group Synthesis: Prototype Participation and Design The FGD contributes four provisional domains without enlarging the questionnaire or rider-record denominators. These are ndings of the narrative synthesis dened in Section 5.4, not newly authenticated participant quotations. Appendix G preserves the full account and verication boundaries. FGD-T1: Listening, practice, and publication. One reported account describes recording privately for self-training and discarding recordings rather than publishing. Private practice may be the intended activity, not failed participation or evidence of anxiety. The label Podcast Paradox remains an analytical shorthand, not a validated construct. FGD-T2: Collaboration and choice. Co-hosting is presented through a peer-conversation and radio call-in rationale. Favourable reactions are reported without attributable extracts or subsequent publishing behaviour. Optional and mandatory co-hosting remain competing choices: an unavailable peer could constrain rather than enable an otherwise willing participant. FGD-T3: Institutional access and visibility. The described ID/PIN arrangement places the proposed service in an ACU context and raises questions about eligibility, privacy, and identiable speech. Membership restrictions do not demonstrate safety, condentiality, or psychometric validity. This FGD does not test EST-P3. FGD-T4: Interface cues and idle content. Proles, timestamps, Boost

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 179 invitations, and fallback music or advertising identify possible coordination mechanisms. Screen interaction alone does not demonstrate comprehension, usability, or improved evidence-based production. 6.7.1 Supplemental Review Without Evidence Promotion The subsequently supplied seven-part generated analysis does not establish new participant ndings. Its suggestions about long-programme preferences and registration feedback are retained as questions within FGD-T1 and FGD-T4, not conrmed experiences or additional themes. Inconsistent translations, unknown speaker roles, and invalid timestamp strings prevent adoption of its bilingual passages as verbatim evidence. Statements of consensus, improved retention, reduced anxiety, safety, or resolved production barriers are not accepted as outcomes. The four domains retain their provisional status; Appendix G.4 distinguishes retained review leads from claims withheld or rejected. 6.7.2 Integration with the Rider Accounts The sources complement one another at the level of questions, not linked cases. The FGD's distinction between listening and publishing resonates with rider accounts of quiet appreciation; collaboration complements accounts of socially local radio; access conditions and interface choices elaborate participatory agency and delivery. These similarities neither merge the codebooks nor prove independent corroboration: source provenance and participant overlap remain unresolved. No FGD theme receives a rider PB score or enters the rider case-coverage chart. The integrated interpretation is that listening, private practice, co-hosting,

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 180 and public publishing may represent dierent goals rather than successive levels of engagement. This motivates competing simulation mechanisms (Section 5.9), not numerical parameters or conrmation of H1H7. The reported duration is compatible with approximately 28 minutes, but a visual timestamp at 30:30 remains inconsistent under a shared time origin. Technical audio gures and unaudited word counts therefore receive no quantitative calibration weight. The new rule-based comparator and LLM-agent extension remain unexecuted. 6.8 Interpretation of Student Rating Impact The empirical evidence concerns students' evaluations of social media radio and the meanings recorded in their accounts. PB is a multi-item experience measure, and its association with stars is convergent audience evidence. Neither measure is a substitute for the Student Rating competence prole in Section 3.7. The survey contains no NMLS item responses or paired competence assessments; consequently no Student Rating treatment eect is estimated from these 52 records. The qualitative analysis nevertheless identies mechanisms relevant to SR: source appraisal and correction in T1, participation conditions in T4, and studentrelevant production interests in T5. These are reasons to examine competence and opportunity directly, not evidence that every participant acquired the corresponding skill. Statements of willingness to create are also distinct from completed, independently assessed media artifacts. The historical model's +.165 star dierence and +.511 PB dierence retain their original interpretation as modelled broadcast evaluations. They are not rela-

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 181 belled as literacy gains, higher Student Rating, or attainment of a level of demonstrated human competence. The next extension uses independent task accuracy as its primary computational outcome and the full NMLS prole only as a secondary synthetic diagnostic. It tests conditional platform eects, not human student development. Its estimands are specied in Section 5.10.12; no future run is included in the reported results. No synthetic pilot-consensus result is included: its raw traces and claimed validation outputs are absent from this archive. A condence proxy cannot establish a measured competence threshold or validate EST. 6.9 Hypothesis Results The H1H7 identiers are retained; H7 now species the prospective computational task test rather than a retrospectively measured eld outcome. Evaluation distinguishes observed associations, conditional simulation contrasts, and direct tests of the specied outcomes. A positive association is not a causal nding, and the absence of a suitable test is not conrmation. 6.9.1 H1: Structural Credibility (EST-P1) The measured starPB association shows agreement between forms of audience evaluation. The model reports ∆PB = +.511 and a star-rating dierence of +.165 under G1 relative to G0. These ndings are consistent with H1's direction, but do not isolate a causal eect of displayed BRS in the eld sample.

These are conditional mechanism outputs. The eld interactionPB association measures neither source-distribution entropy nor an echo-chamber trajectory, and cannot directly establish H2 or a thermodynamic constraint. 6.9.3 H3: Psychometric Validity (EST-P3) The full validity claim in H3 is not established. EST-P3 remains a requirement to test consequential metrics, not a declaration that these instruments have already satised that requirement. Instrument revision must preserve the distinction between perceived credibility, perceived inuence, intention, and independently assessed content quality. High internal consistency (α = 0.957 for the BRS) together with poor singlefactor CFA t is itself diagnostic: it can indicate redundant or overlapping items,

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 183 unrelated method variance, or multidimensionality, and it is not evidence of a good measurement model. Consistent with the calibrated appendix, the thesis therefore reports reliability and structural validity separately, and the ne-grained factor tables are presented with their t indicators visible rather than optimised post hoc. 6.9.4 H4: EST Integration (EST-P1 to P3) The positive associations are compatible with shared variation, but also with overlapping content or common response processes. The Bayesian coecient reported later cannot resolve discriminant validity merely by assigning predictive weight to IQ. H4 receives associational evidence, not conrmation of a unique latent cause. 6.9.5 H5 to H7: Exploratory and Prospective Hypotheses H5 requires repeated participant or network observations to assess convergence, consensus accuracy, or correction dynamics. H6 requires a design separating scheduling from other causes of listening duration; ride duration is not necessarily attentive listening time. H7 requires the planned independent appraisal and production assessments on the agent platform. PB and star-rating dierences are not substitutes for task performance. The present eld survey does not directly test these three outcomes. 6.10 Dual-Framework Hypothesis Testing Report The tables follow the dual-framework discipline of the thesis Results chapter (compact_ch6.tex): every hypothesis is reported rst with the frequentist

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 184 statistics available to a classical reviewer, then immediately with the Bayesian counterpart, and no Bayesian result is presented as proving a frequentist result wrong. Small-sample precision is handled with explicit condence/credible intervals and ROPE statements rather than point rhetoric. 6.10.1 Dual-Framework Hypothesis Table (H1H4) Values in [brackets] are provenance notes, not part of the estimate. Real numbers only; every entry is traceable to a checked artifact. 6.10.2 Sensitivity & Exclusion Audit Table The correlation direction is identical at N = 60, N = 52, and N = 51 (excluding the extreme case SR0018); magnitudes shift slightly. This is the small-sample robustness statement requested by the audit. 6.10.3 Small-N Robustness Memo The retained sample (n = 52, 30 male / 22 female) is small for conrmatory structural modelling, and the thesis does not claim it satises CFA power rules. Three properties keep the reported inference defensible for this design, and each is stated here rather than hidden: 1. Precision over power. The 95% CI on the headline starPB Spearman association is (0.49, 0.80) at n = 52; it excludes a null eect on the null scale, and the same is true of the model contrasts whose replication ranges are reported in ch6.

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS 213 6.12.16 What the Final Experiment Shows The calibrated in-silico experiment shows what the specied design implies. First, the assumed state-outcome weights produce a clear, internally coherent contrast in both evaluative and competence-format Student Ratings. Second, that contrast is accompanied by an assumed engagement cost, which is the central trade-o the thesis argues for.
